\section[a queixa]{a queixa — the complaint (to the police); the grievance}

\label{lesson:PT-C387-queixa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for lawful, then the Portuguese for unlawful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a queixa}
\textbf{a queixa} — \textquotedblleft{}the complaint (to the police); the grievance\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ela apresentou queixa na polícia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She reported it to the police.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Apresentar queixa} — to report something to the police, to file a complaint.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{queixa} is built on \emph{queixar} \textquotedblleft{}to complain\textquotedblright{}, usually traced to Vulgar Latin \emph{quassiāre}, from Latin \emph{quassāre} \textquotedblleft{}to shake\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{quatere} (Lewis \& Short); Spanish \emph{queja} is a cousin (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a queixa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a queixa}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a queixa}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for lawful, then the Portuguese for unlawful, then say \emph{a queixa} again
\end{itemize}

\section[o arguido]{o arguido — the accused, the formal suspect; the defendant}

\label{lesson:PT-C387-arguido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for unlawful, then the Portuguese for the complaint.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o arguido}
\textbf{o arguido} — \textquotedblleft{}the accused, the formal suspect; the defendant\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O arguido não disse nada ao juiz.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The accused said nothing to the judge.}
\end{quote}

A European legal term for someone formally named as a suspect in a criminal case, through to the trial; in Brazil \emph{o réu} or \emph{o acusado}. Feminine \emph{a arguida}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{arguido} is the participle of \emph{arguir} \textquotedblleft{}to accuse, to argue\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{arguere} \textquotedblleft{}to make clear, to prove, to accuse\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o arguido}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o arguido}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o arguido}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for unlawful, then the Portuguese for the complaint, then say \emph{o arguido} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o arguido mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The accused, the formal suspect; the defendant\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[a testemunha]{a testemunha — the witness}

\label{lesson:PT-C387-testemunha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the complaint, then the Portuguese for the accused.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a testemunha}
\textbf{a testemunha} — \textquotedblleft{}the witness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A testemunha viu o acidente da janela.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The witness saw the accident from the window.}
\end{quote}

Feminine in form even for a man: \emph{ele é a única testemunha}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{testemunha} is usually traced to Latin \emph{testimōnium} \textquotedblleft{}witness, evidence, testimony\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{testis} \textquotedblleft{}witness\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); the evidence came to name the person who gives it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the complaint, then the Portuguese for the accused, then say \emph{a testemunha} again
\end{itemize}

\section[a defesa]{a defesa — the defence}

\label{lesson:PT-C387-defesa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the accused, then the Portuguese for the witness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a defesa}
\textbf{a defesa} — \textquotedblleft{}the defence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A defesa pediu mais tempo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The defence asked for more time.}
\end{quote}

Also in sport, the defence.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{defesa} is inherited from Late Latin \emph{dēfēnsa} \textquotedblleft{}defence\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{dēfendere} \textquotedblleft{}to ward off, to defend\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a sentença]{a sentença — the court sentence, the ruling}

\label{lesson:PT-C387-sentenca}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the witness, then the Portuguese for the defence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a sentença}
\textbf{a sentença} — \textquotedblleft{}the court sentence, the ruling\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O juiz leu a sentença.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The judge read out the sentence.}
\end{quote}

Mostly a legal word; a grammatical sentence is \emph{uma frase}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sentença} is inherited from Latin \emph{sententia} \textquotedblleft{}way of thinking, opinion, judgement\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{sentīre} \textquotedblleft{}to feel, to perceive\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
